newsitem.title: ITALY: Italians amused but worried by German gold row.
newsitem.headline: Italians amused but worried by German gold row.

text.p: Italians have reacted to the German government's decision to revalue gold reserves with a grim sense of satisfaction laced with foreboding that Europe's single currency project could now be in danger.

The Bundesbank has attacked a plan by German Finance Minister Theo Waigel to revalue German gold reserves and transfer part of the gains to Bonn, saying it puts at risk the stability of the planned new European single currency, the euro.

The plan ran into a firestorm of criticism from politicians and the press in Germany but in Italy, where governments are used to charges of playing fast and loose with public accounts, political leaders light-heartedly took the moral high ground.

The most telling phrase was attributed by Italian news agency ANSA to Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi, who has orchestrated the government's campaign to qualify for a single currency with the first wave of members in 1999.
"We are no longer the ugly duckling of Europe," Ciampi was quoted as telling political colleagues at a meeting on Thursday.

The Bundesbank row erupted just as Prime Minister Romano Prodi puts the finishing touches to a three-year economic strategy -- a key plank in a do-or-die campaign to take Italy into European economic and monetary union (EMU) in a first wave in 1999.
Former Foreign Minister Antonio Martino said that if Waigel pressed ahead with the gold revaluation plan it would signal a curious role reversal between Germany and Italy.
"Virtue is not proving contagious but quite the opposite," Martino told reporters. "We are not becoming like the Germans but they are becoming like the Italians," he added.
In a light-hearted vein, centrist politician Clemente Mastella said Italy should perhaps consider revaluing its artistic treasures.
"If Germany revalues its gold we can do the same with the country's monuments and artistic beauties, thereby saving the balance of payments," said Mastella.
The government is well aware of the Bundesbank's reluctance to see Italy admitted to a currency union until it has built up a more solid track record of fiscal rectitude.
This has prompted a self-satisfied reaction now German politicians show signs of cutting corners to bolster sagging government finances.

But behind the wry amusement, Italian politicians and journalists could barely disguise their astonishment at the German government's apparent determination to ride roughshod over the most revered central bank in Europe.

"I think revaluing the gold reserves has been judged by all concerned parties as a not correct approach. The Bank of Italy would not accept it and I think European institutions ... would not accept it," said Foreign Trade Minister Augusto Fantozzi.
A deeper Italian concern is that the launch of EMU could be delayed or, even worse, the entire single currency enterprise called off.
Italy, desperate to force down permanently the cost of servicing its huge public debt mountain, has more to gain from EMU than any other country and much to lose if it fails to get off the ground.
Politicans fear all momentum behind efforts to sort out Italy's state finances would be lost if EMU were abandoned or even delayed significantly.

The Bundesbank's objections to the Waigel plan "can influence the selection of the countries joining the single currency, the nature of the Euro, the political outcome of the government and perhaps even the realisation of monetary union itself," said Milan business daily Il Sole 24 Ore.
